2000-summer-olympics: Sydney won the right to host the Games on 24 September 1993, at the 101st IOC Session in Monte Carlo, Monaco. It was selected over Beijing, Berlin, Istanbul and Manchester in four rounds of voting. Brasília, Milan and Tashkent made bids but withdrew during the bidding process. The Games were the first to feature at least 300 events in the official sports program, and the final Games under the IOC presidency of Juan Antonio Samaranch, who was succeeded by Jacques Rogge.

Several quasi-government bodies built and ran the Games, among them the Sydney Organising Committee for the Olympic Games (SOCOG), the Olympic Coordination Authority, which oversaw construction, and the Olympic Roads and Transport Authority. IBM provided technology and Telstra telecommunications. The Olympic torch relay began in Greece and travelled to Australia through a number of Oceania island nations. The organisers treated the project in phases, from positioning in 1993 to 1996 to implementation in 2000 and wind-down in 2001.

A cycle of four arts festivals led up to the Games, beginning with the Festival of the Dreaming in 1997, founded by the artistic director Rhoda Roberts, who later co-directed segments of the Opening Ceremony. The emblem, nicknamed the Millennium Man, was designed by FHA Image Design and showed a stylised torch-bearer with limbs like boomerangs. The official mascots were Syd the platypus, Millie the echidna and Olly the kookaburra. In all, 750 gold, 750 silver and 780 bronze medals were minted, the bronze ones from withdrawn Australian one-cent and two-cent coins.

Teams from 199 countries took part. The United States led the final medal tally, followed by Russia and China, with Australia fourth. Cameroon, Colombia, Latvia, Mozambique and Slovenia won a gold medal for the first time, and Barbados, Kuwait, Kyrgyzstan, Macedonia, Saudi Arabia and Vietnam won their first Olympic medals. The IOC awarded Sydney the Pierre de Coubertin Trophy for the collaboration and happiness shown by its people.

In 2000 the Auditor-General of New South Wales reported that the Games cost A$6.6 billion, with a net cost to the public between A$1.7 and A$2.4 billion, and funds were shifted from education and health programs in the years before. Press reports praised the organisation, and Lord Coe later called the Games a benchmark when London prepared for 2012.
2004-summer-olympics: Athens had lost its bid for the 1996 Summer Olympics to Atlanta on 18 September 1990. Under the direction of Gianna Angelopoulos-Daskalaki it bid again, and the 106th IOC Session in Lausanne chose it on 5 September 1997. The bid drew on the history of the Games and was praised for its low scale, humility and focused message, unlike the 1996 bid, which had been seen as arrogant.

The Greek government spent close to 9 billion euros on the Games. The Athens 2004 Organizing Committee (ATHOC) finished its work as a company in 2005 with a surplus of 130.6 million euros. The Games brought a new airport, an expanded metro, a tram, a suburban railway and the Attiki Odos ring motorway.

The flame was lit at Ancient Olympia on 25 March 2004 and, for the first time, travelled around the world to past and future host cities before returning to Greece. The opening ceremony, directed by the choreographer Dimitris Papaioannou, took place on 13 August and the Games ran until 29 August.

In all 10,625 athletes, about 600 more than expected, took part with 5,501 team officials from 201 countries, in 301 medal events in 28 sports. It was the first time since 1996 that every country with a National Olympic Committee attended. The marathon started in the town of Marathon and finished in the Panathenaic Stadium, and the shot put was held in the stadium at Olympia.

Athens became the fourth city to host the Summer Games twice, with Paris, London and Los Angeles. The United States led the final medal table, followed by China and Russia, and Greece came 15th. Chile, Chinese Taipei, the Dominican Republic, Georgia and Israel won their first Olympic gold medals. The new medal obverse, designed by Elena Votsi, showed the Panathenaic Stadium, replacing a design that had depicted the Roman Colosseum.

The cost of the Games and a possible contribution to the Greek government-debt crisis of 2010–18 has been debated, mostly in popular media, though there is little or no evidence for the claim. A cost-benefit evaluation presented to the Greek Parliament in January 2013 found the net economic benefit for Greece positive.
